en: The Śramaṇa Ji composed this work.

I humbly consider that the six positions are subtle and profound; they rely on the phenomenal world to support the Way and serve as a means to grasp the underlying principle. The two chapters are mysterious and wondrous;

they depend upon the "Obscure" (Mōn) to arrange the categories and explore the pivotal mechanism. How much more so for that which is neither existent nor empty, where all verbal explanations and discriminations come to rest.
Beyond the traces of words,
there is neither arising nor ceasing;
one transcends names and forms at the ford of eternal quiescence.
Ultimate awakening shines far beyond its own source;
the Sage alone discerns its sovereign ruler.
The wordless word stirs like a gale.
Enveloping profound radiance yet dark as the moon,
it is an existence that is not of existence;
its waves surge forth.

When the profound chapters [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] were submerged and the ocean of meaning was no longer accessible, and when the specific manifestations of wisdom failed to unravel the subtle and probe the deep, the definitive meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) was nearly extinguished.
As for the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā*:
[The rest of the text follows.]
This is one of the ten sections,
composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
A white rainbow flies as an ill omen.
The natural grandeur has faded from the landscape;
the subtle and profound meanings have been distorted by the "disordered phoenix," and the sacred texts on palm leaves have fallen into error like the "confused fish."
Reflecting upon it, I see that this treasure of the Dharma and its refined literature were on the verge of falling into ruin;
yet now, with the birth of this one of profound wisdom, his illustrious traces have been transmitted like a lamp,
casting solitary brilliance upon the *Abhidharmakośa*.
He appears to conform to the mundane dust while preaching existence;
he unties the bonds of wisdom through the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
He manifests as unrestrained toward the holy while discoursing on emptiness.
His discernment was all-pervasive and his wisdom universal;
he exhausted the mysteries of the spirit and reached the pinnacle of sagacity.
Having refined his essence through this hymn, he thereby manifested the ultimate mystery.
Before his commentary was completed, he returned to the truth and ascended to the higher realms;
its meaning is vast while its text is concise,
and its fountainhead remains doubly secret.
Thereupon, the ten great bodhisattvas, beginning with Dharmapāla,
purified their minds through sevenfold recitations;
they stirred the river of eloquence to extol these subtle words.
The spirit roams through the eight repositories;
vibrating with golden sounds, it flows forth wondrous exegesis.
Purifying that true consciousness, it brings this elegant treatise to completion.
It is titled the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*,
or alternatively the *Viśuddha-vijñaptimātratā-śāstra*;
its meaning encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate.
It soars high, surpassing the vultures and crags;
its principles penetrate the profound and the ineffable.
It eclipses the dragon palaces and radiates its brilliance.
It summarizes the essential frameworks of all sutras, unraveling the obscure and encompassing the core tenets;
it condenses the refined essence of all treatises, selecting the extraordinary and highlighting the unique.
Its influence flies like the wind, causing the banners of the non-Buddhists to fall.
Since the two causes for the gushing spring [of the Mahayana] would otherwise lead to the chaotic tracks of the Hinayana,
it is therefore modeled after Heaven and Earth so as to carry all beings equally.
It conceives the sun and moon within its womb and radiates brilliant clarity;
how could it merely vie with the Huanghe River for its current or compete with thunder and lightning for its resonance?
In the past, during the Zhou and Qin eras, the profound color of the Dharma was shrouded and the Ultimate Way remained suppressed without being proclaimed.
When the sun of the Han dynasty shed its light, the teachings of the Buddha’s image were disseminated and spread far and wide.
Translators of the sutras, vinaya, and their meanings followed one another in succession, linking their footsteps like a continuous trail.
We frequently encounter the eminent talents of the regions east of the Pamirs, yet rarely hear of the outstanding figures of India. Due to the vast differences in phonology and dialect,
the musical scales of the two lands have become confused,
merging the palaces of the Chinese and the barbarians.
The script was as remote as the heavens;
they were ignorant of its forms and sounds across the Hu and Jin realms.
Although it was but a faint resemblance of dregs and lees, [it remained].
They have not yet been able to fully exhaust the profound mysteries;
the great principles may be at variance, and subtle expressions may lead to misunderstandings.
Vast doubts and major impasses remain, shrouded like mist and coalesced like clouds.
Its profound and brilliant manifestations have appeared repeatedly; the details may be omitted.
Only our own teacher, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang, embodies hidden brilliance and excels above all others.
He illuminates the horizon at the Hall of Spirits,
storing virtue as he dwells in the ancestral seat;
from the pond of wisdom, he surges forth ripples of discourse.
He gallops along the precious tracks of the three wheels,
far surpassing the sands of Jambūnada;
he clarifies the true waves of the eight liberations.
In the pure jade-well of the distant realm,
he forgot his own body to sacrifice himself for the Dharma, entrusting his destiny to the prayer for penetration.
Through a profound resonance with the true nature, he subtly relied upon the cultivation of practice.
It was not that he sought to display his spiritual power or manifest wonders;
rather, he surely harbored blessings and extended auspiciousness.
Having fully trodden the divine traces and exhaustively explored the secret treasuries.
That which the former sages had not yet beheld, they have all penetrated to the pivot of the emotions;
that which the ancient philosophers left behind, they encompass all the ultimate reaches of the mind.
Vowing to propagate and comfort them, I shall now return to my native land.
His virtue simplified the Emperor’s mind and his Way extended the celestial patterns;
thus these precious verses were extolled in the south,
and the golden tablets flowed eastward.
He clarified the principles within the profound ford and dispelled the mists of doubt from his intricate thoughts;
his brilliance surpassed the Tripitaka masters and his mastery exhausted that of any single individual.
Emerging as a preeminent talent from the Five Heavens, his legacy eclipses all of antiquity.
How could he be compared to those whose families relied on the fame of their horses, or who monopolized beauty in the arts of sound and speech?
While Kumārajīva and Dharmaruci spread their fragrance, they were merely celebrated for their mastery of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
It is merely this.
This work originally consisted of ten commentaries collected and categorized;
now, they have been translated in full detail and synthesized into a single volume.
Discerning between the Chinese and Sanskrit,
investigating the nuances of interpretation regarding the light and the heavy,
and refining the distinctions among various meanings.
There is a work by the master Ye Yi,
titled *The Establishment of Consciousness-Only*,
which sets forth the grand framework and proclaims the general title of this entire treatise.
Furthermore, regarding the term "discourse" (lun):
it refers to the distinct titles of the two baskets (piṭaka) as refined and polished mirrors,
and it denotes the designation of that which brings about accomplishment.
It takes establishment as its function;
the term "established by consciousness-only" takes discernment as its meaning.
Only the principle of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) flourishes as the Great Awakening;
the original verses establish the meaning of the Middle Way as being prominent.
"Only" (vimala) signifies a distinction that excludes the existence of external objects.
"Consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to that which is capable of cognizing and designating; it is an internal mind.
The essence of consciousness is explained by the *kevalakarmadhāraya* (appositional compound) as "that which is itself consciousness.
Both the nature and the characteristics of consciousness are not separate from the mind.
Regarding the mental factors and the mind-king, consciousness is primary.
By returning to the mind and dissolving all characteristics, one speaks generally of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
This "only" excludes the existence of external objects.
Those who cling to existence lose their true nature;
those who discern the emptiness of the mind remain attached to it.
Those who stagnate in emptiness deviate from its reality.
For this reason,
those who obscure these [truths of] emptiness and existence remain long submerged in the two extremes;
whereas those who awaken to that which is both empty and existent walk loftily upon the Middle Way.
The thirty verses of this treatise are titled *Vijñaptimātra*.
By means of these, that [reality] is established; thus it is called *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The establishment of consciousness-only serves to manifest the essential purpose of the treatise.
The term *samāsa* (compound) is established based on the *bhartṛparyāya* (the dependent or subordinate member);
the *suvanta* (inflected word) refers to the *svāmiparyāya* (the principal or governing member).
Thus, in this treatise, the proponent and opponent engage like the sounding of drums and banners raised high.
The profound gate opens wide, and the wondrous meanings therein are thus investigated.
One uses the teaching to perfect the teaching;
one relies on the teaching to perfect the principle.
This constitutes a *karmadhāraya* (attributive) compound.
Since it establishes principles through reasoning and establishes the teaching through those principles,
this "treatise that establishes" is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
As for myself, I am but a base scholar;
I am doubly unworthy to take up the brush to serve as a scribe alongside the likes of Rong and Kai.
As my karmic merits have faded and I wander on,
I have mistakenly been included among those who hold the staff and case;
yet, amidst these refined melodies, I truly act as a mere filler among the pipes.
I, an inferior craftsman, have humbly basked in the radiance of those who harbor the jade within;

having been guided by their every instruction in compiling this narrative, I hope that the profound mirror of wisdom will reflect its subtle depths. Thus, I shall now provide a broad exposition of the title.
As for the other specific meanings contained below,
they are each explained individually according to the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot).
The treatise states:
I prostrate to the nature of consciousness-only, the perfectly pure one; I shall now explain that teaching for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
It is said:
To initiate this treatise, it shall be briefly explained by means of five sections:
first, distinguishing the time and the capacity [of the audience] for the teaching;
second, clarifying the fundamental tenet and the essence of the treatise.
1. The inclusion within the Tripitaka and the Vehicles (yāna);
2. The exposition of the year of the teaching and its principal authority;
3. The critical analysis and interpretation of the main text.
First, the discernment of the time and the capacity for the teaching.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the discernment of the time and assembly for the proclamation of the teaching.
Next, the analysis of the capacities of those to whom the teaching is addressed, and the analysis of the assemblies at the time the teaching was spoken:
When the Tathāgata established his teachings, he did so according to what was appropriate for each individual capacity.
These capacities are of three distinct grades.
Consequently, the teaching also differs according to the three periods.
All classes of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), blinded by ignorance (*avidyā*),
give rise to and perform afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma (*karman*).
Deludedly clinging to a self,
they sink without refuge into the ocean of birth and death; therefore,
as soon as the Great Compassionate Honored One first attained Buddhahood, [he acted accordingly].
In the Deer Park, the Rishi turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths;
he preached the Āgamas to eliminate the grasping at a self,
enabling those of lesser faculties and others to gradually ascend to the stages of the noble ones.
Although he has severed his delusion regarding a self upon hearing the Four Noble Truths,
he remains confused by and attached to the notion that all phenomena truly exist.
To eliminate his grasping at the existence of phenomena, the World-Honored One [taught this].
Next, on Vulture Peak, he taught the emptiness of all phenomena,
namely the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and others,
causing those of middling faculties to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and proceed toward the Great Vehicle.
Upon hearing the World-Honored One’s teaching on the profound intent— that non-existence is taught by way of negating existence—
they then repudiated the nature and characteristics of the two truths,
asserting that universal emptiness constitutes the supreme principle.
Because these two sages each clung to existence and emptiness,
their delusions and errors arose in competition, and they failed to realize the Middle Way.
Thus, the Tathāgata acted to eliminate these attachments to emptiness and existence.
In the third period, he expounded the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
such as those in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other assemblies, which state that all phenomena are nothing but consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) and that no phenomena exist external to the mind,
thereby refuting the initial attachment to existence.
It is not that internal consciousness does not exist; rather, by dispelling all attachments, everything is seen as empty.
Free from the extremes of existence and non-existence, one correctly abides in the Middle Way.
Regarding the principle of ultimate truth, there is a specific method for awakening to and realizing it.
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are skillfully able to retain or relinquish [phenomena].
Furthermore, this treatise here cites six scriptures, namely:
the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-guṇavyūha*, the *Abhidharma*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Ghanavyūha*.
The eleven treatises— namely the *Yogācārabhūmi*,

*Prakaraṇāryavācā*, *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, *Daśabhūmika*, *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, *Madhyāntavibhāga*, and *Abhidharmasamuccaya*— are cited as evidence.

Because it clarifies the principle of Consciousness-Only, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the causal stages of practice— thereby fully understanding the characteristics of the Mahāyāna—
it is known that this is the teaching of the Middle Way from the third period.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 76.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* explains its characteristics in detail.
This [classification] distinguishes the three periods according to the gradual teaching methods suited to the capacities and principles of sentient beings.
If the Great Vehicle arises from the Small Vehicle...
There are thus three periods of time, years, months, and sequence.
This refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*’s teaching on *vijñapti-mātratā*.
As for the gate of the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*), it is as follows.
The great does not arise from the small;
thus, there is no sequential order of the three periods of past, present, and future.
This is precisely what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka* as "mind-only."
This was the very first teaching after his initial attainment of the Way;
this refers to the majority of cases.
However, what is clarified in the present treatise applies to both types.
If, for those of indeterminate lineage, the Great [Vehicle] arises from the Small,
it is the teaching of the third period;
if it is intended solely for Bodhisattvas of the Great [Vehicle] and does not arise from the Small, [it is the teaching of the final period].
This refers to the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*).
It demonstrates that there is no fixed distinction between the sudden and gradual teachings,
for even the five hundred *śrāvakas* were present in their seats during the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*).
As stated in the *Śubhākarasiṃha-śrī-mūla-saṃgraha* (The Essential Summary), regarding the discrimination of the capacities of those to be taught:
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, there are five lineages (*gotra*).
The first is the bodhisattva lineage.
Second, pratyekabuddhas;
third, śrāvakas;
fourth, those of indeterminate [lineage].
Fifth, those without lineage (*agotra*).
This treatise’s third [chapter] states:
"Bodhisattvas who have entered the path of seeing are all called 'Victors' (*jina*)."
It is taught specifically because one realizes the ālayavijñāna;
furthermore, it is also taught because prior to the path of seeing, one has already been able to believe and resolve upon seeking that transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti). It further says:
It is called "profound" because sentient beings who lack the spiritual lineage cannot fathom its depths;
those belonging to the lineage of quiescence cannot penetrate it.
Therefore, it is called "extremely subtle.
By virtue of this doctrinal intent,
it applies exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, those bodhisattvas who are of indeterminate lineage are not recipients of the three types of capacities— namely, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and those of no lineage. Therefore,
the capacity for which they are intended must necessarily be of the highest grade.
The profound meaning revealed therein also transcends the two extremes;
its vastness and inclusiveness are difficult to describe in detail.
According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it encompasses five lineages (*gotra*).
Based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, [the Buddha] was attended by members of the four castes;
this differs slightly from the *Śālistambasūtra-śāstra* and other texts,
as explained in the *Jiyao*.
Second, the clarification of the essential body of the treatise.
This section contains two parts.
First, the clarification of the tenets of the treatise.
The subsequent elucidation of the body of the treatise is entirely as explained in the *Shuyao*. To clarify the tenets of the treatise:
there are various classes of foolish persons.
Since beginningless time,
due to the power of the causes and conditions of false discrimination,
one has clung to the notion that there truly exist a grasper and a grasped external to the mind. The Tathāgata, through his great compassion, [bestows] the nectar-like Dharma.
He bestowed [the teaching] upon him, commanding him to take it up.
Thus he severed his deluded and frantic mind, abandoned attachment to emptiness and existence, and realized the definitive meaning of truth.
In the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras, it is taught that all phenomena are nothing but consciousness. — Vasubandhu Bodhisattva.

For the benefit of sentient beings and to ensure that the Dharma endures for a long time, I have composed these thirty verses based on the aforementioned teachings to clarify the principles of Vijñaptimātratā;
their phrasing and meaning are complete and perfect, avoiding both prolixity and brevity. Hereafter follow the commentaries by Dharmapāla and others.
Based on the aforementioned sūtras and śāstras, I have extracted the essential points to provide an extensive commentary on the verses; thus,
it is titled *Cheng weishi* (Establishing Consciousness-Only),
and for this reason, it takes Consciousness-Only as its central tenet.
"Consciousness exists and is not empty;
objects do not exist and are not real"—
this is established as our thesis.
Although it is clear that all phenomena do not exist apart from consciousness, regarding the elucidation of its essential nature,
this is explained according to the eighty-first section of the first part, the *Viniscayasamgrahani*, of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The essence of the sūtra is twofold:
first, the text;
second, the meaning.
The phonemes (*vyañjana*) are the basis, and their meaning (*artha*) is that which depends upon them;
for it is by means of the expressive phonemes that the meaning is revealed.
Thus say the masters Sthiramati and Asvabhāva.
This means that through the power of the Buddha’s compassion, original vows, and conditions,
for those capable of hearing, mental images of words and meanings arise within their own consciousness, appearing as if the Tathāgata were speaking.
These mental images of words and meanings—
Although it arises through the power of one's own reliance on roots of goodness,
it is called "the Buddha's teaching" with respect to its original conditions;
yet in reality, the Buddha has no speech.
If this is based on the fundamental [nature], there is neither text nor meaning;
there is only untainted great samādhi, wisdom, and compassion.
If it is based on one's own consciousness:
When a contaminated mind manifests,

it takes as its essence the appearance of the words and meanings of the uncontaminated; when an uncontaminated mind manifests, [it likewise takes as its essence the appearance of the words and meanings].
It takes as its essence the true, untainted words and meanings;
this is precisely why the Tathāgata did not, in reality, preach the Dharma.
Thus, it is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 425, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, and other texts.
The Buddha himself has declared that since his attainment of Buddhahood,
he has not uttered a single word;
you likewise have heard nothing.
The treatise states that what appears as a collection is its very essence;
this is precisely the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Thus says one master in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding this interpretation, Dharmapāla, Yaśomitra, and others state:
"Alternatively, through the power of the causes and conditions of the original vows of those worthy of hearing [the teaching],
the aspects of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of the Tathāgata."
In reality, its essence consists of the words and meanings that constitute the signifier and the signified.
If one speaks according to the fundamental [truth],
its essence consists of the true, untainted words and meanings.
Therefore, the sixty-fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* quotes the *Śukṣepapatra-sūtra*, stating:
"That which I have not yet spoken is of such extent. This is also stated in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Through the successive force of mutual reinforcement,
the two consciousnesses become determinate;
therefore, the Blessed One truly teaches the Dharma.
The statement "it is not spoken" is a teaching of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).
Since the root of this treatise is the Buddha’s sūtras,
the definition of its essential nature (*svabhāva*) should be according to what is taught in those sūtras.
Although there are these two explanations,
since this master of the treatise does not fail to teach the Dharma,
one should adopt the latter interpretation. Generally speaking, there are four levels for determining the essential nature (*svabhāva*) [of the treatise].
First, subsuming characteristics back into their nature:
all have "thusness" (tathatā) as their essence.
Therefore, a sutra says:
All phenomena are also suchness;
even unto Maitreya, they are suchness.
These two [categories] subsume objects within the mind.
All is representation-only (vijñapti-mātra).
As it is said in the sūtras, "The three realms are mind-only.
These three [categories] subsume the provisional according to the real.
Just as with non-associated [factors] and the states of matter and mind,
the Abhidharma treatises state that these are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
Thus, the four natures are explained according to their distinct functions.

Matter and mind are each subsumed under their own respective categories, whether provisional or substantial; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the aggregate of matter subsumes those ten bases in their entirety. Thus concludes the second and fourth sections above.
That which is transformed by one's own consciousness constitutes the second [category], which subsumes objects within the mind;
this is also stated to be the teaching of the Buddha.
This is the fourth section, the distinct discussion of the functions of the natures.
To the listener, it appears as a dharma; to the speaker, it is the true teaching.
Both are the equal outflow from the pure dharmadhātu.
Speaking in terms of the fundamental [principle], this teaching also takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence.
This constitutes the first [method]: subsuming characteristics back into their nature.
All names and so forth that can be spoken or heard are merely vocal modulations;
apart from sound, they have no intrinsic substance.
Therefore, when a designation follows its substantial basis, it is itself sound.
This is the third [category], the inclusion of the conventional according to the real.
The Abhidharma-śāstra states: "Sound produced by formation refers to the speech of the noble ones."
Although the four bodies emerge with differing aspirations,
from the perspective of ultimate principle they do not contradict one another;
such is the nature of this treatise.
If it arises from the transformation of a contaminated mind based on what has been heard,
or from the contaminated words and meanings of a speaker,
it belongs exclusively to the dependent nature (paratantra-lakṣaṇa) and is subsumed under names and so forth.
The transformation of the untainted mind,
or what is called the untainted,
is subsumed under correct knowledge and pertains to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Because untainted conditioned phenomena (anāsrava-saṃskṛta) pertain to both natures,
the essence denoted by this consists of the object of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra), correct practice, and the fruit.
If one can express the essence,
it consists of sounds, names, and so forth;
although the body of the sutra is twofold.
Now, we take the sounds, names, phrases, and so forth that are capable of expressing meaning, because they constitute the essence of the true teaching.
Question: Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), fifteen are contaminated (*sāsrava*).
How is it that sound and the others are also included within the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
The three—names, phrases, and phonemes—are by nature indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

How can it be said that they also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the wholesome (*kuśala*)? Answer: This is according to the perspective of the "conforming transformation" (*anuvartana*), referring to the bodies of those of the two vehicles and others.
It is taught that fifteen [factors] are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
while names (*nāman*) and so forth are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is according to the present Mahāyāna.
If it is only the sound, names, phrases, and syllables of the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata subsequent to [enlightenment] that are truly wholesome and untainted,
the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that both the speaker and the listener rely on two factors.
First, sound; second, excellent syllables.
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "My Dharma is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*), whereas yours is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This treatise’s second [chapter] speaks of the two unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena (*dharma*) and expression (*nirukti*).
There is a distinction in their objects:

the dharma-āyatana has names and so forth as its object, while the vyañjana-āyatana has sounds as its object. Furthermore, this is stated in the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra and the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, chapter seventy-eight.
In the ninth stage, two types of delusion are abandoned:
first, the delusion regarding mastery over dhāraṇīs concerning the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables of immeasurable teachings;
as this treatise’s ninth [stage] states: "immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables."
This is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). Furthermore,
this treatise and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* state that the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) include those that are untainted and wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*).
Therefore, taking the teaching as its essence does not contradict reason. Question:

If it is clarified that the essence of the teaching is entirely *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), why then is it said to be "spoken by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas"? Answer: As Vasubandhu explains in his commentary:
Because it is a matter of predominant arising, he spoke thus. Regarding the "Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only," Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
"Through the successive power of predominance, the two consciousnesses become established."
This means that because of the differentiation of consciousness within one continuum, it causes the arising of differentiated consciousness in another continuum;

this is due to their acting as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another. Question: Since the past and future are not substantially existent, how can they serve as such conditions?
It is not that conditioned phenomena abide immediately after arising;
how then can the understanding produced by hearing the teachings be gathered? In response, Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyā* states:
"It occurs sequentially upon the consciousness of the listener during the eight stages."
It has as its essential nature the manifestation of a collection of direct and indirect speech; that is to say, because during the eight occasions,
a collection of both direct and indirect speech manifests upon the consciousness of the listener.
As stated in the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, fascicle 81:
"All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent;
they possess the nature of arising and ceasing."
Because that which is born must necessarily perish,
its cessation is bliss— just as when one utters various syllables,
the mind immediately gives rise to seeking.
Continuing from the initial resolve,
although it consists of many moments (*kṣaṇa*),
its practice and understanding are of a single nature, collectively termed "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*).
Because one has not yet definitively ascertained all that is being perceived.

Therefore, one should make a distinction. According to the treatise:
because one severs the afflictive obscurations that cause the continuity of rebirth, one realizes true liberation.
"By severing the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) through the analytical knowledge that removes hindrances, one attains Great Enlightenment.
The commentary states:
This indicates the distinct severance of both the obstructions and their results.
There is separate proof.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 59:
"All afflictions are capable of continuing rebirth."
These are precisely the afflictions that initiate karma and moisten rebirth;
in this treatise, they are all termed *saṃyojana* (fetters). "Vrana" has the meaning of agitation, and "nāna" has the meaning of confusion.
Because they agitate and confuse sentient beings, they are called *kleśa* (afflictions).
Only the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa) initiates karma and moistens rebirth;
its nature is that of a binding dharma.
This is not the case for the cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa).
Therefore, the statement regarding "continuing birth" refers solely to the afflictions (*kleśa*). As for that which is called "liberation," its essence is *parinirvāṇa*.
In the Indic language of the Western Regions, it is pronounced *parinirvāṇa* (the word *nirvāṇa* should be read with a departing tone). Here, *pari* means "complete" or "perfect."
The term *nirvāṇa* means "quiescence," which signifies the sense of the perfect body of quiescent extinction.
The older translation "Nirvana" is a corruption and abbreviation of this sound.
Now, following ancient usage, it is also called *nirvāṇa*.
It has many names, as found in the fifth chapter of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*.
This is explained within the context of the lower transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Because sentient beings are bound by the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they perpetually dwell in birth and death;
once they have realized parinirvāṇa, they are able to leave those bonds behind, and thus the name "liberation" (*vimukti*) is established.
The essence of liberation is not identical to the category of resolve (*adhimokṣa*).
"Resolution" (*vi-muc*) means to be free from bondage;
"liberation" (*vimukti*) means mastery.
The "obstruction" (āvaraṇa) refers to the afflictions (kleśa), thus it is called the "affliction-obstruction" (kleśāvaraṇa).
This is an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (possessive compound).
It obstructs and conceals nirvāṇa, preventing one from approaching its realization.
The various practices cultivated by ordinary beings are merely temporarily extinguished;
the ascetic austerities of non-Buddhists are reckoned as realizing nirvana;
and even the afflictions up to the Peak of Existence are merely temporarily severed.
The principle thus revealed is grasped as parinirvāṇa;
it is now explained that this is merely a partial nirvāṇa.
Although the principle is called "true," because the seeds [of affliction] are not severed, it is not true liberation.
Furthermore, although those of the two vehicles and others attain the two types of cessation, [they do not attain true liberation].
Abiding within these two is not non-abiding;
liberation is not real because it is merely conventional.
The realization of suchness in the ten stages is not yet true liberation;
to distinguish it from those [stages], it is called "true liberation.
Its provisional substance is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Reality is precisely *tathatā* (suchness),
because it is manifested by the extinction that leaves no remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirodha*).
Furthermore, it is distinguished from the liberation attained by non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles, both in its totality and its particulars.
To speak of "true liberation" is merely a conventional designation,
for it does not exist as something that fails to abide.
One immediately abandons the afflictions and separately attains nirvāṇa.
As for "the knowable," it refers to all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, because they are all objects of knowledge.
The wisdom that thoroughly understands what is knowable is called "liberation. "Obstruction" has the meaning of "hindrance."
The category of attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) obscures the objects of knowledge,
obstructing right understanding so that it cannot arise. What is called "right understanding" is another name for perfect awakening (samyag-bodhi).
In Sanskrit it is called *bodhi*, which is translated here as "awakening" (*jue*),
because one awakens to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
*Mārga* means "path."

Because it traverses the meaning [of the path], the ancient saying that "the path of bodhi" [refers to this] is incorrect. Because the category of attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) obscures the objects of knowledge (jñeya), preventing wisdom from arising, it is called the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa).
This establishes the name "obscuration" based on that which is obscured;

it is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound meaning "the obscuration of the knowable. Second, the essence of that which is obscured consists of the four categories of wisdom (*jñāna*).
And the four nirvāṇas.

These will be explained in detail later in the section on the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may practice the contemplation of the two kinds of selflessness and such as the *tathatā*, their [realization] is not "Great" Bodhi;
the wisdom of the two vehicles is Bodhi, but it is not "Great. Furthermore, although ordinary beings and non-Buddhists possess some slight wisdom, [it is not Great].
It is not great enlightenment.

their enlightenment is not great.
Now, by distinguishing it from that [other], it is called "Great Bodhi.

the wisdom of the bodhisattvas is great but not bodhi.

Because the wisdom of ordinary beings is neither of these two types. Question: Regarding the statement that the two obstacles each obstruct one fruit, do they specifically obstruct them individually, or can they also mutually obstruct one another?
Answer: This is not fixed; they may either obstruct individually or obstruct mutually.
In this context, the individual obstacles are explained because they specifically obstruct meditative concentration;
this will be understood in detail below. Furthermore, the interpretation that there are those who are deluded or mistaken regarding the two kinds of emptiness [is as follows].
Regarding the phrase "because there was delusion and wrong view when one had not yet entered the Dharma, [one now] gives rise to correct understanding":
this refers to the periods of the two stages— the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*)— prior to entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Although one has not yet attained realization,
because one deeply believes in and contemplates the mind, understanding arises;
this is the first stage, the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Since all accumulations are preparatory practices (*prayoga*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speaks of only four stages.

On the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one generates resolute belief solely by following what has been heard. Generating this understanding is for the purpose of severing the two heavy obstructions.
This reveals the entry into the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are distinguished as being "heavy obstructions.

This is the second stage, the Stage of Thorough Penetration (*prativedhāvasthā*). Through the abandonment of the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*), those obstructions are successively severed.
It is revealed that within the stage of the path of cultivation across the ten bhūmis,
all [afflictions] are rooted in the two obstacles and the two types of grasping;
throughout these ten bhūmis, one realizes emptiness and eliminates obstacles until reaching the ultimate stage.
This is the third stage, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Regarding the phrase "cutting off hindrances in order to attain the two supreme fruits":
this reveals that the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) cuts off the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realizes true liberation.
Because one attains bodhi by severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), this is precisely the fourth ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*). The preceding text has already explained this.
Thus far, the first [section] has demonstrated how, through the arising of understanding and the severance of obstructions, one attains two superior fruits.
Furthermore, there are various interpretations,
as explained in the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot).

there are others who are confused and mistaken regarding the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*).

Due to conventional designation,

Based on the transformations of consciousness, one gives rise to grasping by taking deluded mental states as conditions.

Based on internal deluded perceptions, they are spoken of as "self" and "dharmas.

it might be confused with the seventh [consciousness].
It should be said that these six [consciousnesses] which discern coarse objects are called "consciousnesses that discern objects" (*ālambana-vijñapti-vijñāna*),
because they discern coarse characteristics,
thereby distinguishing them from the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses].
The discernment of objects is consciousness;
this is also explained as before. This is according to the ultimate among ultimates, where both mind and speech are utterly transcended.
According to the second and third ultimate truths,
it cannot be described as either one or many;
because they are real, their characteristics are not distinct.

The commentary states:

That is to say, the single substance of consciousness transforms and manifests as two parts—
image and seeing— arising like a snail producing two horns.
This explains the image-aspect and the seeing-aspect.
Apart from its substance, there is no separate nature,

this would mean dividing the vision— which is the very meaning of the self-substance— into [separate] functions.
Therefore, there are no distinct seeds apart from the substance of consciousness itself;

With consciousness as its support, it transforms the seeds of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) and arises as the semblance of the object-phenomena.
Because their natures differ according to their distinct functions,
the theory of distinct characteristics and distinct seeds is superior from the perspective of principle.
Therefore, it is said that the substance of consciousness transforms and appears as two parts. This dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is non-existent yet appears to exist;

because it is not actually two parts but appears as the two parts—the subject and object—of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), it is designated with the term "appearing. If the characteristics are distinct and possess their own seeds, why are they called the transformation of consciousness? Because they are not separate from consciousness.
Because characteristics arise only when consciousness undergoes transformation,
just as the derived matter arises from the primary elements;
because the objects of the characteristic arise from the conceptualizing mind.
The mind arises only when there is an object;
therefore, it is not that there is only the object, but rather we speak of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
This reveals the two divisions of the transforming [consciousness]: the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).

If the function and the substance exist separately, why is it said that consciousness arises appearing as two parts? [The Treatise says: The function and the substance do not exist separately. Why? Because consciousness arises appearing as two parts. How so? It is because the nature of consciousness is such that it manifests as two aspects. What are these two? They are the aspect of the object (*grāhyākāra*) and the aspect of the subject (*grāhakākāra*). Just as a single face appears as two when reflected in a mirror, so too does a single consciousness arise manifesting as two parts. Therefore, it is established that the substance of consciousness is one, while its functions appear as two. Thus, there is no fault in saying that consciousness arises appearing as two parts. Furthermore, if the substance were separate from the function, then when the function ceases, the substance would remain; yet, since the substance of consciousness is momentary, it perishes simultaneously with its function. Therefore, we know that the substance and function are not distinct entities. Consequently, it is taught that consciousness arises appearing as two parts. This concludes the explanation.
Because the mutual perception of both arises based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
The commentary states:
If self-cognition did not exist, these two [cognitions] would certainly not arise.
Just as horns certainly do not exist when there is no head,

Therefore, it is said that the two parts arise based on the substance of consciousness.
This collectively demonstrates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The above has demonstrated what is transformed by consciousness.

"Transformation" means that the substance of consciousness transforms and appears as two divisions;

Because one does not realize that phenomena lack true existence, due to the grasping at dharmas,
that which appears as the two parts arises; specifically, that which appears as the imagined nature is reckoned as the dependent nature.
The two divisions do not exist as separate entities;

which exists as if it were present despite being non-existent.
That is to say, the minds of the three natures all possess attachment to dharmas.
The self-substance of the eight consciousnesses each manifests as two parts,

Second, the substance of the ears does not exist;

This is cited from the final section of the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa* composed by Vasubandhu.
It is taught that the member of ignorance is admitted to pervade all three natures;
therefore, with the exception of the Tathāgata, all [minds] possess two parts, which are considered to be the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Question:

If these two parts are non-existent in essence, how does the essence of consciousness transform to appear as these two parts? Answer: Because both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).
Because the self-substance of consciousness is characterized by false habitual tendencies,
because it is not in accordance with reality,
and because there is attachment to it.
Because it is associated with ignorance,
it transforms and appears as two parts;
these two parts are precisely the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) and the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga).
It arises based on the substance of consciousness.
Because that substance is delusory, it transforms into what appears as two divisions.
These two divisions are said to arise based on self-cognition; if the substance of consciousness did not exist, these two divisions would also not exist.

Therefore, the arising of the two parts exists by virtue of the substance of consciousness. Since both the self-substance and these two parts exist, upon which part are the self and phenomena metaphorically designated?
Answer: The self and phenomena are provisionally established based on these two parts.
Based on these characteristics and views regarding the imagined nature,
the world and the sacred teachings speak of "self" and "dharmas.
Within these characteristics and views, all are said to be self and dharmas.
Because both self and phenomena are devoid of these characteristics, there is nothing upon which they can rely.
Therefore, based on the apprehended characteristics, one designates the two divisions of self and phenomena through perception.
The Blessed One is able to know the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) as well as suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is beyond words and is neither self nor dharma;
it is for the purpose of eliminating the real self and dharmas clung to by the ignorant that [the teaching] is established upon the two divisions transformed by that consciousness.
The designation "self" and "dharmas" is a conventional expression used as a skillful means to lead [beings] to understand that it is a mere convention;

"For what reason are my [Buddha’s] teachings based solely on two parts, rather than conceiving of a self-entity as the self and the phenomena? Answer: According to the explanation of Dharmapāla:
According to the actual facts, it is also reckoned thus;
for now, let us take the two transformed parts as the basis.
It is not that there is no basis for the reckoning within its own substance.
Briefly, there are three reasons why it is not mentioned:
first, because [the two types of] grasping are pervasive;
second, because the grasping at a self does not arise based on self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).

it is simply stated that the two aspects (dvaya-bhāga) subsume the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka).
